items.title: Neodesha Business Honored at Kansas Business Awards
items.summary: A local business is honored at the 2026 Kansas Business Awards. This year’s annual awards ceremony was held Thursday in Overland Park and the winner of the Mainstreet Momentum Award for southeast Kansas went to Carver Home, Office, and Furniture Outlet or CHoFO of Neodesha. The store offers new and open-boxed furniture for homes and businesses and is located on Neodesha’s Main Street. The Mainstreet Momentum Award honors businesses that actively work to revitalize downtown areas and commercial districts through ongoing growth, investment, and community engagement. CHoFo is located in one of Neodesha’s historic buildings, one that formally housed one of the Ben Franklin's Five-n-Dime stores as well as once being the home of a bowling alley. ChoFo officially opened its doors in Neodesha on May 8th of this year. Photo: (l to r) Neodesha Community Development Director Chris Bauman, Miranda Carpenter, CHoFO Proprietor Larry Carver, Kansas Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of Commerce David Toland, Neodesha Mayor Devin Johnson, and Neodesha City Administrator Brogan Jones. Courtesy City of Neodesha

items.title: Suspect Arrested in Baxter Springs Stabbing
items.summary: A suspect is in custody in a weekend stabbing in Baxter Springs. Baxter Springs Police and Cherokee County Sheriff’s deputies responded to a Saturday night report of a stabbing in the 300 block of East 11th Street. Upon arrival at the scene, the victim was located and found to be suffering from multiple stab wounds. The suspect fled the scene before law enforcement arrived but was soon located walking along US-69 Alternate just north of the city. The suspect was taken into custody and identified as 23-year-old Tramone Howard-Hill of Baxter Springs. He was transported to the Cherokee County Jail and booked for Aggravated Battery with a Deadly Weapon. Police also learned that Hill had an outstanding warrant out of Shawnee County, Kansas, for Electronic Solicitation of a Child. The victim in the case remains hospitalized in critical condition. This investigation is ongoing and formal charges will be submitted to the Cherokee County Attorney’s Office. The Quapaw Nation Marshal Service and the Galena Police Department also assisted on the case.

items.title: Chanute Breaks Ground on New Wastewater Treatment Plant
items.summary: The City of Chanute breaks ground on its new wastewater treatment plant. The groundbreaking ceremony took place on Thursday, October 8, as the City undertakes a $36 million project to modernize its outdated wastewater treatment plant. The move is part of a major overhaul and upgrade of Chanute's municipal infrastructure. The existing wastewater treatment plant was put online in March 1983, but the facility no longer meets modern regulatory standards and a major overhaul has been delayed since 2010. New construction includes a new lift station, motor-control centers, electrical/control systems, and site-wide grading, paving, and process piping integration. The project bid was awarded to Crossland Construction of Columbus. In addition to the wastewater plant, Chanute is pursuing a simultaneous $26 million upgrade to its drinking water treatment plant. Photo courtesy Chanute Chamber of Commerce

items.title: Oklahoma Man Dead in Thursday Crash
items.summary: A 77-year-old Afton, OK, man has died following a single-vehicle crash on Thursday afternoon, according to the Oklahoma Highway Patrol. Troopers identified the man as James Fuser. Authorities say Fuser was driving southbound on County Road South 520 near East 230 Road when his vehicle left the roadway to the left. The vehicle then crossed three barbed-wire fences before striking an embankment. The crash occurred at approximately one p.m. Fuser was pronounced dead at the scene by medical personnel. The Highway Patrol reports Fuser died as a result of a medical event. No additional information about the circumstances surrounding the crash was immediately available.

items.title: Sedan City Council Hears Recap of Fur Harvesters Convention
items.summary: The Sedan City Council hears a recap of the recent Kansas Fur Harvesters Convention. The convention was held in Sedan last weekend at the Chautauqua County Fairgrounds and has played an important part of the City's tourism and economic goals. Sedan Chamber of Commerce Secretary Priscilla Ellis says the event drew a large group to the City. The Council also voted to approve a $965 reimbursement to the Chamber for promotional items. The Chamber says the items can also be used for other events to promote the City. In other business, The council approved street closures on October 31 st for the Halloween Carnival and the Trunk-or-Treat.

items.title: Kansas Man Arrested After Police Pursuit in Northeast Oklahoma
items.summary: A Baxter Springs, Kansas man is facing multiple charges following a police pursuit that began in Miami, Oklahoma, Wednesday evening. Miami Police say an M-P-D officer stopped a motorcycle near 20th Avenue Northwest and F Street Northwest around 6:15 p.m. The rider, identified as Samuel Reffett, allegedly presented a driver’s license belonging to another person before fleeing on the motorcycle. Officers pursued Reffett through northwest Miami. Police say he reached speeds of about 100 miles per hour. Due to the speed and heavy traffic, the pursuit was terminated for public safety. Reffett later encountered Quapaw Nation deputy marshals and again fled, leading to another pursuit. The chase ended when Reffett crashed the motorcycle on East 50 Road. He tried to flee on foot but was taken into custody. Reffett was not seriously injured. Investigators also determined the motorcycle had been reported stolen in Cherokee County, Kansas.

The decision presents two distinct questions that divided the court: whether the proposed tax exemption conflicted with existing constitutional rules governing property taxation, and whether the Supreme Court should decide such a constitutional question before an initiative has been enacted by voters at all. By Miami News-Digest In January 1944, with the United States still fighting the Second World War, President Franklin D. items.title: 43rd Annual Pelican Festival at Grand Lake
items.summary: Grand Lake welcomes the pelicans back as 43rd annual festival returns to Grove GROVE, Okla. — One of northeast Oklahoma’s most recognizable signs of autumn is returning to Grand Lake — and this weekend, an entire festival is being held in its honor. The 43rd Annual Pelican Festival runs Thursday through Sunday, Oct. 1-4, at Wolf Creek Park in Grove, bringing together carnival rides, live music, food trucks, arts and crafts, classic vehicles and excursions onto Grand Lake to see the enormous white birds that inspired the celebration. The festival is organized around the seasonal migration of the American White Pelican, which passes through the Grand Lake region during the spring and fall. Festival organizers say the birds can be seen around the lake from roughly September through November during their fall movement. They are difficult birds to overlook. American White Pelicans are among the largest flying birds in North America. Cornell Lab of Ornithology measurements put their wingspan at roughly 8 to 9½ feet, with adults distinguished by their massive yellow-orange bills, white bodies and black flight feathers visible when their wings are spread. items.title: Before "Sooner"
items.summary: Before “Sooner” Became a Namesake of Pride: Indian Territory, the Land Runs, and the Making of Modern-Day Oklahoma The word “Sooner” is now inseparable from Oklahoma identity. Its original meaning was considerably different. The first Sooners were people who entered land before the federal government legally opened it for settlement, violating rules designed to give prospective claimants an equal starting time. The land itself lay within Indian Territory, amid treaty-established Native nations whose governments, boundaries, and property rights had developed through removal, war, negotiated agreements, federal coercion, and decades of political struggle. I. Oklahoma Did Not Begin With the Land Run At noon on April 22, 1889, thousands of people surged into approximately 1.9 million acres in central Indian Territory. The event became one of the enduring images of Oklahoma history: horses running across prairie, wagons bouncing over rough ground, railroad passengers pouring into improvised towns, and homesteaders driving stakes into the earth. items.summary: WHEN THE GOVERNMENT BECOMES PART OF THE DRUG TRADE Controlled buys, informants and controlled deliveries can expose criminal networks. Documented cases also show what happens when the line between investigation and participation breaks down. There is an uncomfortable paradox at the center of modern narcotics enforcement. Government exists, in part, to prevent dangerous drugs from reaching the public, yet some of the investigative techniques used to accomplish that purpose necessarily place police officers, confidential informants, money, firearms, and sometimes controlled substances inside the very commerce government is attempting to suppress. A confidential informant may be instructed to purchase fentanyl. An undercover operative may negotiate a drug transaction. Investigators may permit a package of apparent narcotics to continue toward its destination so that they can identify the recipient. Police may conduct a controlled sale or delivery rather than immediately terminate a transaction. Each practice can produce evidence that would otherwise be difficult to obtain. MIAMI, Okla. — The central question surrounding civil asset forfeiture in Oklahoma is considerably larger than what happens to cash found during a traffic stop. It can involve the family car. It can involve a pickup truck, aircraft, boat, or even farm equipment. It can involve firearms. It can involve land and the improvements standing upon it. Under Oklahoma's controlled-substances forfeiture law, qualifying vehicles and other conveyances, real property, money, and weapons may all be subject to forfeiture. In a contested proceeding involving those categories, the state generally bears a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard. Oklahoma law also contains protections for qualifying innocent owners, mortgagees, lienholders, and other interests. What happens after forfeiture makes the system unusual. items.summary: Of Dust, Copper, and Breath Matter, Life, Consciousness, and the Soul I. Matter Matter is the physical substance of the world: stone, water, metal, bone, blood, and the bodies of living creatures. Chemistry commonly distinguishes between organic compounds, associated chiefly with carbon chemistry, and inorganic materials, which include metals, minerals, salts, and many other substances, although the boundary between these categories is not absolute. Neither term should be confused with living or nonliving, because living organisms depend continually upon inorganic substances such as water, calcium, iron, sodium, phosphorus, and potassium. Human bone itself joins an organic collagen framework to an inorganic calcium-phosphate mineral phase, demonstrating that life does not inhabit a chemical realm separated from the mineral world. The more important question, therefore, is not merely what substances an organism contains, but how those substances are selected, ordered, maintained, and made to serve the unity of the living whole. items.title: When Prosecutorial Discretion Becomes a Commodity
items.summary: When Prosecutorial Discretion Becomes a Commodity Oklahoma history shows why no prosecutor should have the final, unreviewable power to decide when the criminal law will—or will not—be enforced MIAMI, Okla. — Prosecutors need judgment. They decide whether evidence is sufficient, whether witnesses are credible, what charges fit the facts, whether a plea agreement serves justice and whether limited public resources should be spent pursuing a case. But there is another side to prosecutorial discretion that receives far less attention. A prosecutor also possesses the power not to act. The power not to charge. The power to reduce a charge. The power to dismiss. The power to decline a referral. The power to decide that conduct which might ordinarily result in prosecution will go no further. Usually, those decisions are legitimate exercises of professional judgment. But Oklahoma history demonstrates something that should concern every citizen regardless of politics: Discretionary criminal-justice power has value. And anything with value can be corrupted. items.summary: When the Racket Gets a License How Northeast Oklahoma’s old vice economy may have evolved from illegal protection into legal control There is an old American crime story that usually ends the same way. The bootlegger buys a legitimate business. The gambling boss becomes a developer. The fixer becomes a political donor. The man who once needed the sheriff to look the other way learns that it is safer to own the building, hire the lawyer, obtain the license, influence the regulator, cultivate the prosecutor and let the law itself define who may compete. The mob, as the trope goes, “goes legitimate.” Northeast Oklahoma has a documented history that makes that question unusually difficult to dismiss. In the early 1970s, federal courts exposed an illegal gambling and protection conspiracy centered around the Grove-area club known as Mr. Yuk. The scheme involved local nightclub interests, Kansas City figures, District 13 District Attorney Lewis Frank Grayson and his investigator George Husong.
